The first art galleries were dark. The painted chambers of Chauvet and Lascaux lie far beyond the reach of daylight, in corridors that can only be entered by crawling or by the grace of a guide with a lamp. The people who decorated them did not have to go there. There were entrances, overhangs, sunlit rock faces where any passerby could stop and look. Instead, thirty thousand years ago and more, they carried fire down into the earth — small sandstone lamps burning animal fat, flames a few inches tall — and painted lions and rhinoceroses and running oxen on walls no sunlight had ever touched. The flickering light made the animals move. Perhaps that was the point. Whatever it was, they chose the dark, again and again, across thousands of years. The oldest human images were made in a place where seeing was an act of effort, patience, and one small flame.

For nearly all of human history, night was a genuine condition, not the absence of one. Light was scarce enough to be measured in individual candles, and a single candle barely pushes back the dark past arm's length. When the fire guttered out, the night outside was total — a blackness we can barely reconstruct, softened only by the moon and by stars bright enough to cast faint shadows. Night had geography and weather, an etiquette, a population: spirits, saints, thieves, lovers, the dead. Some people worked in it — bakers, watchmen, midwives — but for most it was a country you entered at dusk, and the crossing changed you. Sounds sharpened. An owl was an event. A lantern in a distant field was a signal, a question, a small impossible sun.

The historian Roger Ekirch spent years digging through diaries, court records, medical texts, and letters from the centuries before cheap light, and he found something strange: nobody slept through the night. Or rather, nobody expected to. Across centuries and languages, documents refer to the "first sleep" and the "second sleep" as naturally as we say lunch and dinner. Between them lay an interval — an hour, sometimes two — that people simply lived in. They rose to tend the fire, pray, read, make love, visit a neighbor, or lie still and think. Old French even had a word for this hovering state: *dorveille*, sleep-wake, the mind half-surfaced and lucid. The midnight hour was not insomnia. It was a room in the house of night, and people furnished it.

In the 1990s, a researcher named Thomas Wehr tested whether this was cultural habit or buried biology. He placed volunteers in extended darkness — fourteen hours of it, mimicking a natural winter — for a month. After a period of confusion, their sleep split in two, precisely as the old documents described: a solid stretch of sleep, then a quiet hour or two of calm wakefulness with its own distinct hormonal profile, then sleep again until morning. The midnight waking, which we now treat as a disorder to be medicated, may simply be an old human rhythm asserting itself whenever it gets the chance. Our bodies remember the long night even though our cities have forgotten it.

Then came the flood. For most of history, light was ruinously expensive; an hour of lamplight could cost the better part of a day's wages, which is one reason night was respected. Whale oil, then gas, then the arc lamp — a light so violent that observers compared it to lightning caught in glass — then Edison's filament, and finally the twentieth century, which did to darkness what it did to silence and wilderness. An economist named William Nordhaus once traced the price of artificial light across history and found that it had fallen by a factor so large the numbers stop meaning anything: today, less than a second of average labor buys an hour of brilliant light. We went from hoarding candle stubs to blanketing continents in glow, in about six generations.

Look at the earth from above now, on any clear night: it is lit like a circuit board. The light leaks upward, scatters off air and dust, and pools into what astronomers call skyglow — domes of haze over every city that bleach the stars out of the sky. A landmark 2016 atlas concluded that four in five North Americans, and a third of all humans, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Worse, the tide is still rising. One recent analysis of satellite and citizen-science data found the night sky brightening by roughly ten percent a year — meaning a child born today will live under skies more than twice as bright as the ones her grandparents knew. The change is so recent that we have had no time to understand what we traded away. Darkness may now be the most underprotected commons on earth.

Because we think of darkness as mere absence — light, interrupted — we assume nothing lives in it. The opposite is true. Darkness is a habitat. It has residents, economies, migrations, love affairs. By most estimates the majority of mammal species are nocturnal, along with uncountable billions of insects, and they are not merely tolerating the night. They are adapted to it the way a fish is adapted to water: eyes rebuilt, senses reordered, whole lives scheduled around ten or twelve hours of rescue from the sun. When we brighten the night, we are not adding a little light to a neutral void. We are flooding someone's homeland.

Consider the sea turtle. Hatchlings dig out of their nests at night and race toward the brighter of the two horizons, which for a hundred million years has meant the ocean, moonlit and glittering, against the dark dunes behind. A beachfront hotel changes the equation. The porch light is brighter than the sea, and so thousands of hatchlings every year turn inland, crawl toward highways and pools, and die under lights that were, from their point of view, the most convincing ocean in the world. Coastal towns now pass dark-sky ordinances, dimming their bulbs during nesting season — a small, late confession that darkness is infrastructure, as real as a road, and that we paved over it without looking.

Or the birds. Most songbirds migrate at night, steering by stars and by the faint signatures of the earth's own light. Over Manhattan each anniversary of September 11, two beams rise from lower Manhattan in memory of the towers, and on migration nights researchers have documented thousands of birds funneling into the beams, circling in the glow as though it were a false dawn, spending the energy they need for their journey. One study estimated that the beams bent the paths of more than a million birds across just a handful of nights. The operators now watch the counts and douse the lights for twenty minutes at a time — and the birds scatter back into the dark within minutes. That is often how easy the fix is. The dark was fine. We only have to stop breaking it.

Even the moth at your porch light is not being foolish; it is being wrong-footed by geometry. Entomologists long assumed moths steered by the moon, mistaking the bulb for a celestial landmark and spiraling helplessly into it. But high-speed camera studies published in 2024 suggested something stranger: an insect near a light reflexively tilts its back toward the brightness, the way it would tilt toward the open sky, and so it stalls, loops, and tumbles around the lamp like a plane caught in a downdraft. The porch light is an illusion of "up." Fireflies, meanwhile, court by light — precise, species-specific flash patterns exchanged in darkness — and the ambient glow from streets and yards drowns the signal. In lit areas courtship fails, and in some places the fireflies thin away, year over year. We call it a decline. It is closer to a silencing.

We are creatures of the same rhythm whether or not we admit it. In darkness the pineal gland secretes melatonin, and the body begins its long night shift of maintenance — repairs, housekeeping, the filing of memory. A phone screen at midnight does not merely entertain you; it is a message to your biology that the sun is up. Shift workers, who live their lives under artificially daylit nights, pay for it in elevated rates of heart disease, diabetes, and certain cancers. We have not abolished night. We have only, badly, rearranged it, leaving ourselves with the costs of darkness and none of its benefits.

And yet the old night is still out there, a few hours' drive from most cities, waiting. In January 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles in the middle of the night, and something odd happened: people went outside, looked up in alarm, and reportedly called 911 and the local observatories to ask about a vast, strange, silvery cloud hanging over the darkened city. It was the Milky Way. Enough of them had never seen it — had never once seen the galaxy they live inside — that their calls read like reports of a UFO. That is what four generations of light can do: not just hide the stars, but make them unbelievable.

Stand under a truly dark sky and the first thing that fails is scale. The sky stops being a ceiling and becomes depth — you are not looking *at* it, you are looking *down into* it, and the stars stop being points on a dome and become suns at wildly different distances stacked into darkness. From a dark place you can see a few thousand stars; from a city, a few dozen. The Milky Way itself resolves from a smear into a structure, a tilted river of light with dark channels running through it, and in the very darkest places on earth it is said to be just bright enough to cast a faint shadow. Give your eyes half an hour and they rebuild themselves: a pigment in the retina called rhodopsin regenerates, your sensitivity climbs enormously, and you learn the trick of averted vision, seeing faint things by looking slightly beside them.

Under that sky you can, with no instrument at all, see the Andromeda galaxy — a smudge above and away from the river, actually a trillion stars gathered two and a half million light-years distant. The light entering your eye that night left Andromeda before our species existed. You are not looking at the universe's present; you are looking at its deep, deep past, unmediated, with the same naked equipment your ancestors used. For a couple hundred thousand years, the Milky Way was humanity's most shared document. Every culture read it: a river of heaven, a road of souls, an emu gliding across the Australian sky, milk spilled from a goddess's breast — the word "galaxy" literally means milky circle. It was one text no one could ban and no one could edit, visible from every latitude on the planet. Losing it is not like losing a view. It is like losing a language everyone used to speak.

There is also what the dark does to the mind. Everyone knows the three a.m. self: more honest, more frightened, more inventive than the daytime version, half-dissolved and strangely reasonable. We say we fear the dark, but notice that what we fear is never darkness itself — darkness cannot touch you, cannot see you, wants nothing. What we fear is what the imagination stages in it. The dark is a theater, and we bring our own plays. Yet the old records of the second sleep suggest the midnight hour was not spent in dread; it was spent in prayer, conversation, reflection — the quietest thought of the day, surfacing in a lucid half-wakefulness that almost no modern person gets to experience. Mystics went further, describing the divine through darkness — the divine dark, the cloud of unknowing — on the theory that light is already a kind of statement, and darkness leaves room for what no statement can hold.

For most of our history, stories were told in darkness. The fire ring, the dark pressing in beyond the light, the audience's faces half-lit — this was the native medium of fiction. Images could appear there precisely because the eyes had nothing else to do; deprived of scenery, the mind supplies its own. Which loops back to the caves. They painted where it was dark, I think, because the dark is where the images live — because a picture under steady daylight is a thing, and a picture in flickering firelight is an event, an animal that moves. Our first galleries were dark because that is where seeing and imagining stop being different activities.

And here is the last turn: you have never actually seen light. What you call seeing happens in the dark. The eye is a small black room; light enters through the pupil and dies on the retina, its energy translated into tiny electrical whispers that travel down the optic nerve into the brain — which is itself sealed in absolute darkness, no light reaching it ever, under any circumstances. Every dawn you have ever watched was finally viewed inside a wet, lightless chamber behind your face, reconstructed there in the dark. Darkness is not the opposite of sight. It is the venue.

So when the lights go out — when the grid fails, or the campsite is far enough out, or the storm takes the streetlights down and the night stands up to its full height — it is not the world ending. It is the world, uncovered. Underneath our glow the old night is intact, the same darkness the cave painters carried their lamps into, the same one your ancestors woke in at midnight, unafraid, to tend the fire and think. We spend so much effort lighting the darkness, as though it were a defect in the design. But the dark was never the absence of the world. It is the room we see it in.
